content.text: Imaging techniques can be used to investigate the body.

A claim of the form 'have a scan and live longer' mixes two separate questions: what the scan is able to show, and what harm the scan itself may do. Answer both, and only then say whether the claim is justified.

For the PET image, follow the chain: a tracer is taken up by the target cells, the tracer is radioactive, its nucleus decays and emits a positron, the positron meets an electron, and the machine detects what comes out of that meeting rather than the original emitted particle.

items: (c)(i) The claim cannot be justified as stated. A CT (CAT) scan produces cross-sectional images by rotating an X-ray tube and detector array about the patient and reconstructing the images from the differing attenuation of X-rays by air, fat, soft tissue and bone. It is fast, non-invasive, and excellent at locating fractures, tumours, haemorrhage and the position of catheters, so it saves lives by enabling correct and early diagnosis and treatment. However each scan delivers an ionising dose of typically 5-10 mSv, comparable to several years of natural background radiation, so it carries a small but real risk of inducing cancer, and the iodine contrast medium required for many studies can cause allergic reactions and can damage the kidneys. A CT scan is a diagnostic test, not a treatment, and it does not itself prolong life; any benefit comes from the medical decisions the scan enables.

(c)(ii) A positron-emitting tracer such as fluorine-18 labelled fluorodeoxyglucose is administered and is taken up preferentially by cells that are metabolically active, so the tracer concentrates in the target tissue. Where the tracer's radioactive nuclei decay, each nucleus emits a positron and a neutrino. The positron travels a short distance through the tissue, slows to rest and then annihilates with an electron, converting the pair's mass into two gamma-ray photons of equal energy travelling in opposite directions. A ring of detectors records these coincident pairs, and the line joining each pair shows where the annihilation happened, so a tomographic image of the tracer distribution, and hence of glucose metabolism, is built up. Detecting the two photons in coincidence also gives good depth information and allows most of the single gamma rays to be rejected, so the technique is highly sensitive.

content.text: Part (c)(i) is a justification question, so the structure has to be argument rather than description. The first step is to set out what a CT scan actually is: a rotating X-ray tube and detector array records many projections of the body from many angles, and a computer reconstructs cross-sectional images from the differences in X-ray attenuation between air, fat, soft tissue and bone. That establishes the uses: it is a fast, non-invasive, high-contrast way of locating fractures, tumours, haemorrhage and catheters, and because it is fast it allows life-saving intervention, for example in a stroke or a serious abdominal injury. The second step is the cost side: it is ionising, with a typical effective dose of 5-10 mSv, several years of background radiation, so it carries an increased lifetime cancer risk, and it usually requires an iodine contrast injection that can trigger allergic reactions and renal failure. The third step is the judgement: since the scan only produces information, and the benefit flows entirely from the medical action taken as a result, the statement 'have a CAT scan and live longer' confuses diagnosis with treatment and is an overstatement. A fair version would be that CT scans greatly increase the chance of surviving serious disease because they allow it to be found and treated early.

Part (c)(ii) is a chain of physics, and each link must be present. The tracer is chosen so that the target organ takes it up preferentially, so the radioactivity that follows is concentrated where the metabolism is; fluorine-18 labelled fluorodeoxyglucose is taken up by cells using glucose. Unstable nuclei such as fluorine-18 decay, and this particular decay is by positron emission: a proton converts into a neutron and a positron is produced, together with a neutrino which leaves undetected. The positron is slow-moving, so before it stops it travels millimetres to a centimetre or two in tissue. It then annihilates with an electron, and because the pair has zero net charge the two gamma-ray photons must be emitted in exactly opposite directions, each carrying at least 1.022 MeV, the pair's rest energy. Detectors arranged in a ring around the patient register the two photons arriving simultaneously in opposite directions, and the intersection of the line joining them with the body locates the annihilation event. Accumulating many such locations by coincidence and tomographic reconstruction produces the image, whose brightness maps the density of the tracer and therefore the glucose metabolism. The two-photon detection also rejects most of the uncorrelated single gamma rays, which is why PET can detect the very low activities involved.

content.text: Describe the sequence of events and associated processes of physics by which an image is produced using magnetic resonance imaging.

An MRI image is not formed from rays that arrive; it is reconstructed from a signal. Work in this order: align the nuclei, disturb them, detect their response, and then work out where in the body the response came from.
For the disturbance and the response, remember that a magnetic field splits the available energy levels of a nucleus, and that the radiation involved is at a frequency fixed by that splitting.

For the position information, note that the magnet is not uniform: the field strength, and therefore the frequency of the signal, varies with position, and that is exactly what lets the signal be located and then computed into an image.

The patient lies in a strong uniform main field $B_0$, which aligns the magnetic moments of the hydrogen nuclei in the body's water and fat with the field. A pulse of radio-frequency radiation at the Larmor frequency $f_0 = \frac{\gamma B_0}{2\pi}$ is applied perpendicular to $B_0$ and rotates the net nuclear magnetisation away from the field. When the pulse is switched off the nuclei precess about $B_0$ and relax back towards equilibrium, and the rotating net magnetisation induces an alternating signal in a receiver coil. Gradient fields applied during detection select a slice and encode the other two coordinates, because the local field strength, and hence the signal frequency, varies with position. Computer Fourier transformation separates the signal into its component frequencies, and therefore into positions, so a set of cross-sectional images of the proton density of the body is produced, with the weighting of the $T_1$ and $T_2$ relaxation times determining the grey level.

The whole process rests on one piece of physics: the interaction of nuclear magnetic moments with a magnetic field. Hydrogen-1 has a non-zero nuclear spin, so each nucleus behaves as a tiny magnet with magnetic moment $\mu$. In the main field $B_0$ the moments occupy two quantised energy states, aligned with the field (lower) and opposed to it (higher), separated by $\Delta E = h\gamma B_0$, where $\gamma$ is the gyromagnetic ratio. With a large enough field the population difference between the two states is appreciable, which is what makes an NMR signal possible at all.

A radio-frequency pulse of exactly the resonance frequency $\omega_0 = \gamma B_0$ is absorbed by the nuclei and tips the net magnetisation out of equilibrium, so the sample acquires a transverse component. With the pulse off, the ensemble of spins precesses coherently about $B_0$ at $f_0 = \gamma B_0/2\pi$, about 42 MHz per tesla for hydrogen, so a 1.5 T scanner operates at 64 MHz. The transverse component then decays as the spins lose energy to the surroundings, which is described by the longitudinal recovery time $T_1$ and the spin-spin time $T_2$. Because different tissues have different $T_1$ and $T_2$ values, weighting the signal by them produces the grey-level contrast in the image.

The precessing magnetisation induces a small alternating voltage in a receiver coil placed around the patient, by Faraday's law applied to a rotating dipole. The measurement problem is that the coil senses the whole sample at once, so position must be encoded separately. That is the job of the gradient fields: because the frequency of a given nucleus is proportional to the local field, switching on a gradient while the signal is being received gives every position its own frequency. A Fourier transform of the detected signal then sorts the signal into a map of position, and repeating the measurement in three orthogonal directions, for a stack of slices, builds the image. This is why the images are inherently tomographic reconstructions rather than direct photographs.

content.text: Telescopes are used to observe astronomical objects.
Both words describe a telescope but they are not the same thing: one asks how faint a source can be seen, the other asks how close together two sources can be and still be told apart.

For the second part, decide which technique is limited by the wavelength of the radiation being collected. Anything that depends on the reflecting surface being optically perfect is irrelevant if the wavelength is very long.

(i) Sensitivity is the ability to detect faint light or photons; resolution is the ability to separate two closely spaced objects in an image, independent of how bright they are. (ii) Only interferometry is useful for a radio telescope. A radio telescope has poor resolution because the wavelength it collects is very long, but it already has good sensitivity from its large collecting area. Interferometry combines signals from widely separated collectors, so the resolution is set by the maximum baseline rather than by the dish diameter, giving a very large improvement, and the added collecting area improves sensitivity moderately. Active optics is not useful because the tolerable errors in the reflecting surface are very large at radio wavelengths, and a radio dish is a light, stiff structure that deforms negligibly when it is slewed, so its shape never needs active control.
Resolution and sensitivity are independent properties of an instrument: a small telescope can be sensitive but poorly resolved, and a large one can resolve well while missing faint sources.

The angular resolution of any single aperture is limited by diffraction, $\theta \approx 1.22\lambda/D$, so for the metre-long wavelengths of radio waves even the largest single dish gives hopeless resolution. Interferometry removes that limit by combining the signals from two or more collectors separated by a baseline $B$, so the resolution becomes $\theta \approx \lambda/B$ with $B$ of hundreds to thousands of kilometres; radio telescopes on opposite sides of the Earth can be combined in real time. Sensitivity improves too, because the effective collecting area is the sum of the areas of all the dishes linked, though that is only a modest gain since areas add rather than baselines.

Active optics exists to hold the surface of an optical mirror within a small fraction of a wavelength of perfect figure while the mirror is steered and while temperature and gravity deform it. A radio dish needs none of that: at metre wavelengths the allowed surface error is of the order of many wavelengths, the dish is a light and stiff mesh or panel structure rather than a thick glass mirror, and the forces that distort an optical mirror are negligible at that scale. Active optics can therefore improve neither the resolution nor the sensitivity of a radio telescope.

content.text: The colour of a star gives information about its temperature.
Work out $B - V$ first and think about what a positive value means, remembering that magnitude is logarithmic so a LARGER magnitude is a FAINTER flux.
For the measurement, name the two filters, the detector and the subtraction - the colour index is a difference of two magnitudes, not a colour.

(i) More red. $B - V = 4.6 - 2.9 = 1.7$, a large positive colour index: the visual magnitude is smaller, that is the star is brighter in V than in B, so the star is relatively faint in blue and bright in the visual band, i.e. redder than the Sun. (ii) A photodetector or CCD at the telescope records the star through a blue (B) filter and again through a visual green (V) filter. Each exposure gives an apparent magnitude, and the two are subtracted to give the colour index $B - V$, a single numerical value that can be compared between stars.

(i) $B - V = 4.6 - 2.9 = 1.7$. Because magnitude is defined as $m = -2.5\log_{10}(F/F_0)$, a larger magnitude means a smaller flux, so $V = 2.9$ corresponds to a brighter flux than $B = 4.6$. The star therefore emits relatively more red light and less blue light than the Sun, which is what a large positive colour index means and what the question is asking for.

(ii) The telescope's photometer or CCD is exposed through a blue filter calibrated to the standard B band, and again through a green filter calibrated to the standard V band, in the same position on the sky and under the same conditions. Each exposure yields an apparent magnitude; the colour index $B - V = m_B - m_V$ is their difference. Subtracting removes the overall brightness of the star and leaves a number that depends only on its spectral distribution, so values can be compared directly between stars and used to assign a colour and hence a surface temperature.

content.text: Describe the advantages of using photoelectric technologies over photographic methods in photometry.
Compare the two methods on the things that matter when you are measuring many faint stars over long periods: sensitivity, how the signal is recorded, and whether the data can be re-analysed.
For each advantage, say what it lets the observer DO that a photographic plate does not.

Photoelectric photometry is more sensitive, so much fainter stars can be measured; its response is linear and easily calibrated against standard stars, so the magnitudes are more accurate; the readings are recorded electronically and can be stored, reduced and re-analysed, and the telescope can be operated remotely and in real time, so long-term repeat monitoring is practical; and narrow-band filters give better spectral discrimination. Photographic plates must be exposed, developed and fixed in a laboratory, take time, and cannot easily be stored or re-measured against a different calibration.

A photographic plate records photons in an emulsion, so every measurement needs an exposure, then chemical development and fixing, then measurement on a measuring machine. That is slow, the plate has to be handled and stored physically, and re-analysing the same plate later under a different calibration is impractical. A photoelectric photometer converts the light into an electrical signal immediately, so a magnitude can be produced and logged in real time, and the telescope can be pointed and read remotely.

The remaining advantages follow from the same conversion. The output current or count rate of a photodiode or photomultiplier is proportional to the incident intensity over a wide range, so after calibration against standard stars the magnitude is more accurate than a plate measurement, and the much lower threshold means fainter stars are within reach. Because the response is defined by a filter rather than by an emulsion, narrow bands can be used, giving better spectral discrimination than the broad response of a plate. The one respect in which plates retain the advantage is spatial resolution, which is why the two methods have largely complementary roles.

content.text: Describe the sequence of events and the associated physical processes a star undergoes in moving from A to B to C.

Read the three labelled points off the diagram before writing anything: A lies on the upper, cooler part of the main sequence, B lies on the main sequence slightly hotter and brighter, and C lies on the giant track above it.

For each move ask two questions: what is the source of the energy that balances gravity in the core, and what does that do to the star's radius and temperature? The direction of travel on the diagram follows from those two answers.
Keep the sequence ordered and explicit - the marks are for a logical progression from gravitational collapse, to core hydrogen fusion, to core helium fusion.

A is a protostar: a cool molecular cloud has collapsed under gravity, converting gravitational potential energy into thermal energy, and the star moves down and to the left onto the main sequence as it heats up and settles into equilibrium. At B the core is hot enough for hydrogen fusion, mainly the proton-proton chain $\mathrm{H} \rightarrow \mathrm{He}$, and the star is a stable main-sequence star. When the core hydrogen is exhausted the core contracts and heats further, the hydrogen-burning shell expands and cools, and the star moves up and to the right to C, a red giant; at C the core is hot enough for helium to fuse to carbon in the triple-alpha reaction, which is then the source of the energy balancing gravity.

Position A sits on the upper, cooler part of the main sequence. The star has only recently formed by the gravitational collapse of a cold molecular cloud; as it collapsed, gravitational potential energy was converted into thermal energy, so the protostar heated up while contracting. Outward pressure from that heat progressively halted the collapse, and the star settled lower and further left on the diagram, becoming denser and hotter, until at B it reached hydrostatic and thermal equilibrium.

At B the core temperature has reached roughly $10^{7}\,\mathrm{K}$, so hydrogen nuclei in the core fuse to helium, mainly through the proton-proton chain. The energy released by this fusion provides the outward pressure that balances the inward gravitational pressure, so the star is stable on the main sequence and remains there for most of its life, slowly converting H to He in the core.

When the core hydrogen is exhausted, fusion in the core stops. Gravity then exceeds the outward pressure, so the core contracts; the contraction converts gravitational potential energy into heat and the core temperature climbs. The shell outside the core, still rich in hydrogen, heats up until it too begins to fuse hydrogen. The expanding, cooling shell causes the star to swell and its surface temperature to fall, so on the diagram the star moves up and to the right, arriving at C - a red giant, larger, cooler and far more luminous than at B.

At C the contracting core has reached a temperature of order $10^{8}\,\mathrm{K}$, high enough for helium to fuse: three helium-4 nuclei combine in the triple-alpha reaction to form carbon, releasing energy that again balances gravity and stabilises the core. Fusion in the core is therefore the process that holds the star at each stage, and the switch from hydrogen fusion to helium fusion is what produces the change in the star's size and luminosity that the path from B to C shows.

content.text: Marsden and Geiger conducted an experiment in which they fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most of the particles passed straight through.
Two outcomes of the gold foil experiment need explaining - the large number of undeflected particles and the small number of large-angle deflections. Each constrains the model in a different way.
For the second part, name the two specific failures of Rutherford's classical orbits before you describe how Bohr's postulates removed them.

(i) Rutherford's model has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting at a distance, leaving most of the atom as empty space. Empty space explains why nearly all alpha particles passed straight through with little or no deflection, and the small fraction that came close to the tiny nucleus, where the electric field is enormously strong, were deflected through very large angles. (ii) Problem 1: a classical orbiting electron has a continuous centripetal acceleration and should radiate electromagnetic energy, so it should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus - yet atoms are stable. Bohr's answer: electrons occupy only certain stationary energy levels and do not radiate while in them. Problem 2: Rutherford's model cannot explain the discrete line spectra emitted by excited gases. Bohr's answer: energy is emitted or absorbed only in discrete quanta $E = hf$ when an electron moves between levels, so each element emits its own characteristic lines.

About 1 in 10 000 alpha particles was deflected through more than $90^{\circ}$. A diffuse cloud of positive charge, as Thomson proposed, could not do this, because the field it would produce over atomic distances is far too weak. Large-angle scattering requires a concentrated charge, and the observed dependence of scattering angle indicates a single region of charge and mass, tiny compared with the atom, which Rutherford identified as the nucleus.

The second outcome sets the complementary constraint. Because almost every alpha particle passed through undeflected, the mass of the atom cannot be mostly material that interacts strongly with the alpha particles, so the positive charge and nearly all the mass must be confined to that very small nucleus and the remainder of the atom must be mostly empty space containing the electrons.

Two problems then follow. First, classical electrodynamics says a charge undergoing continuous centripetal acceleration radiates; an electron in a classical orbit would radiate continuously, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in about $10^{-11}\,\mathrm{s}$, which contradicts both the stability of atoms and the observed line spectra. Second, even if the electron did not radiate, Rutherford's model offers no mechanism for the discrete frequencies in the emission spectrum of hydrogen. Bohr resolved both by postulating that electrons may occupy only certain non-radiating stationary energy levels, and that energy is exchanged only in quanta $E = hf$ when an electron moves between levels. That single set of postulates accounts for atomic stability and for the characteristic spectra at the same time.

content.text: Electrons can be shown to have wave-like properties.
de Broglie's argument rests on treating light's energy and its momentum with the wave and the particle formula at the same time and asking what the two have in common.
Davisson and Germer's result came from an accident with their vacuum tube. Ask what had to happen to the nickel surface before a diffraction pattern could appear at all.
For the calculation the de Broglie relation connects wavelength to momentum, so isolate the velocity - and check your powers of ten, because the result is far below $c$.

(i) de Broglie proposed that, just as light combines wave and particle behaviour, matter does too: from $E = hf$ and $p = hf/c$, both $E$ and $p$ depend on $f$, so a particle of momentum $p$ should behave as a wave of wavelength $\lambda = h/p = h/mv$. (ii) Davisson and Germer were reflecting electrons from a nickel target when a crack let air into the tube and the nickel surface oxidised; after heating it to remove the oxide they accidentally grew large nickel crystals, larger than their electron beam. Electrons then diffracted from these crystals in exactly the way predicted by de Broglie's relation, confirming that matter has wave properties. (iii) $v = 2.2\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

(i) Light exhibits wave and particle behaviour simultaneously. de Broglie noted that the wave model gives $E = hf$ while the photon model gives $E = pc$, so $hf = pc$ and hence $f = pc/h$. Interchanging the roles of photon and particle, a particle of momentum $p$ is associated with a frequency $f = p/h$ and therefore with a wavelength
which is not observable for macroscopic particles because $h$ is so small, but is significant for the much lighter electron.

(ii) Davisson and Germer were studying the reflection of electrons from a nickel surface. A crack in their vacuum tube allowed air in and the surface oxidised; when they heated it strongly to remove the oxide they instead produced nickel crystals bigger than their electron beam. The reflected beams then showed interference fringes, and the wavelengths deduced from the fringe spacing followed de Broglie's relation. Diffraction is a wave phenomenon, so the experiment confirmed that electrons have a wave nature.

content.text: Nuclear stability can be related to binding energy.
Mass defect is a difference between two masses - be careful which is larger, and say why.
For the graph, the quantity on the vertical axis is already an average PER NUCLEON. Read it at both mass numbers and then ask which nucleus needs more energy per nucleon to break up.

(i) Mass defect is the difference between the total mass of the separate free nucleons that make up a nucleus and the actual mass of the nucleus: $\Delta m = m_{\text{constituents}} - m_{\text{nucleus}}$. (ii) The nucleus of mass number 50 has the greater average binding energy per nucleon, about $15\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$, than the nucleus of mass number 200, about $14\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$, so the nucleus of mass number 50 is the more stable of the two.

(i) The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of the free protons and neutrons that form it, because energy is released when the nucleons bind and that energy itself carries mass, $E = mc^{2}$. Hence $\Delta m = m_{\text{constituents}} - m_{\text{nucleus}} > 0$, and the mass defect is the mass equivalent of the energy that would be required to pull the nucleus apart.

(ii) Reading the curve: at mass number 50 the average binding energy per nucleon is close to the peak of the curve, about $15\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$, while at mass number 200 the curve has fallen to about $14\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$. The average binding energy per nucleon measures how tightly the nucleons are held and therefore how stable the nucleus is, so the mass-number-50 nucleus, with the higher value, is the more stable of the two. Note that the total binding energy, which is this value multiplied by the mass number, is much larger for the heavier nucleus; it is specifically the average per nucleon that indicates stability.

content.text: In 1920, Rutherford suggested the existence of an undiscovered nuclear particle.
Explain how Chadwick confirmed Rutherford’s prediction using conservation laws.
Chadwick had two things to establish: that the extra radiation really was a particle, and what its mass and charge were.
Both follow from the same experiment if you assume the collisions were elastic and then apply conservation of momentum and conservation of kinetic energy to them.

Rutherford had predicted a neutral particle of about the proton mass. Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and found that in addition to the expected carbon nucleus a second, previously unknown radiation was emitted. He collided this radiation with light nuclei of known mass, such as hydrogen, and measured the speeds they acquired. Treating the collisions as elastic and applying conservation of momentum and conservation of kinetic energy gave a mass for the unknown particle close to the proton mass but with zero charge, so the radiation was shown to be a particle - the neutron - rather than electromagnetic radiation.

Alpha particles striking beryllium produce carbon plus an unknown product. Chadwick tested the nature of this product by letting it collide with hydrogen and nitrogen nuclei and measuring the speeds those nuclei acquired. If the collisions were elastic, conservation of momentum gives $m_1 v_1 = m_1 u_1 + m_2 v_2$ and conservation of kinetic energy gives $\tfrac{1}{2}m_1 u_1^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}m_1 v_1^{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}m_2 v_2^{2}$; eliminating $v_1$ between the two equations fixes the ratio $m_2/m_1$ from the measured speeds of the struck nuclei.

The values obtained were close to unity for every target nucleus used, so the unknown particle has a mass comparable to a nucleon. Electromagnetic radiation, which carries negligible mass, could not transfer momentum in this way and could not produce that result, so the radiation was shown to be a particle rather than a wave. Repeating the momentum balance with the known target masses then showed that the particle carried no charge, while its mass was almost identical to that of the proton. That confirmed Rutherford's 1920 prediction of a neutral particle of about the proton mass: the neutron.

content.text: Theories and experiments not only help increase our understanding but also generate new questions.
Use the standard model of matter to support this statement.
Use the standard model's own content - the matter particles, the force-carrying bosons and how the forces are mediated - rather than a list of particles.
The second half of the question asks for questions the model still raises. Choosing two or three genuine open problems and saying why each is a problem shows the model generating new questions.

The standard model says all matter is made of six quarks and six leptons, and that the three interactions between them are mediated by exchange particles - gluons for the strong force, the photon for the electromagnetic force and the W and Z bosons for the weak force - so accelerator experiments test it and it explains the composition and behaviour of matter extremely well. It also raises new questions: why there are exactly six quarks and six leptons; why their charges take the values they do; how the particles acquire mass, which the Higgs boson only partly answers; and why gravity, described by general relativity, cannot be included, since the standard model is a quantum-mechanical model.

The standard model has been developed out of both theory and experiment. Early linear accelerators and cyclotrons were the tools that revealed the composition of matter, and today synchrotrons and machines such as the LHC provide the high energies needed to create and study the particles themselves, so predictions such as the W and Z bosons and the Higgs boson have been confirmed experimentally.

Its content explains a great deal. Matter is built from a small number of elementary particles: six quarks, which combine into the hadrons, and six leptons, of which the electron, muon and tau and their neutrinos are observed in the laboratory. Three forces act between these particles and each is carried by its own exchange particle - the gluon, the photon and the W and Z bosons - which is why the interactions can be described quantitatively, and why the observed behaviour of scattering and decay can be predicted and tested.

The model also generates new questions, and these are its continuing strength as well as its limitation. Why are there six quarks and six leptons rather than one, or seventeen? Is there a single deeper particle from which the different quark and lepton charges follow? The standard model contains no mechanism that generates the observed masses of the quarks and leptons, which is why the Higgs boson was predicted for decades before it was found, and why the origin of mass is still not fully explained. And because the standard model is a quantum-mechanical model it cannot be reconciled with Einstein's general theory of relativity, so the gravitational force is not part of it. Each of these is an active field of research, which is exactly the statement the question asks to be supported.

(iii) Open loop: there is no feedback path from any comparator output back to its inputs, so each comparator saturates to the supply rails. (iv) $O_1 = D_2 + D_1$ and $O_0 = D_2 + \overline{D_1}D_0$, giving the truth table below, where X means the value of that input does not affect the output.

The tap $V_t$ sits between the second $1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor and the bottom $0.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor, so its potential above ground is the drop across that $0.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor:
For reference the other two taps sit at $2.5\,\mathrm{V}$ and $4.17\,\mathrm{V}$, giving three roughly evenly spaced comparison levels, which is what a 2-bit converter needs.

With its very large gain an open-loop op-amp output is driven to whichever supply rail the sign of $V_{in} - V_{\text{tap}}$ demands, so the output is $5\,\mathrm{V}$ for a 'high' comparison and $0\,\mathrm{V}$ for a 'low' one, a clean logic level.

content.text: Electronic systems use transducers.
Decide the direction of energy flow for each device: is it taking energy from the thing being measured, or supplying energy to the thing being controlled?

For the glasshouse table, work through the three quantities one at a time and, for each, name the transducer, say whether it is an input or an output, and describe in one sentence what changes inside it.
A relay is worth thinking about carefully: the small current that operates it and the large current it switches are in different circuits.

(i) An input transducer takes energy from the quantity being measured and converts it into a signal the rest of the system can process; an output transducer takes energy from the system and delivers it to the environment, so that the system can influence it. (ii)

rows: The resistance of the LDR, or the current produced by the cell, changes with the light level falling on it, giving an electrical signal that represents the sunlight.
The resistance of the thermistor changes with temperature, giving an electrical signal that represents the temperature.
A small current through the relay electromagnet pulls the contacts together, switching the much larger current that drives the pump.

content.text: (i) Transducers are the interface between an electronic system and its environment. An input transducer measures an environmental characteristic: it absorbs energy from that characteristic - light, heat, sound, pressure - and converts it into an electrical signal, so nothing is drawn back from the measured quantity into the circuit. An output transducer works the other way: it draws energy from the circuit and converts it into a form the environment responds to, so the system can act on the world. Many components can be configured as either, depending on which side of the interface they are used.

(ii) Sunlight intensity is an input. An LDR's resistance falls as the light level rises, so in a potential divider with a fixed resistor the light level is converted into a measurable voltage; a photovoltaic cell would instead give a current proportional to the light level.

Temperature is also an input. A thermistor's resistance changes with temperature - falling for an NTC device - and in a potential divider with a fixed resistor this produces a voltage that represents the temperature.

The pump is an output. The controller cannot supply the current a pump needs, so the pump is driven through a relay: a small control current energises the relay's electromagnet, which attracts an armature and pulls the contacts together, closing a separate circuit that carries the larger current to the pump. The relay also keeps the two circuits electrically isolated. The glasshouse system therefore needs two transducers of the measuring kind and one of the acting kind.

content.text: Outline the differences between digital and analogue signals using the operation of a music CD player as an example.
The essential distinction is between a quantity that can take any value in a range and one that can take only a small number of allowed values.
For the CD player, trace the signal path and ask at which points the signal is stored as a pattern of digits and at which points it is a continuously varying voltage.

A digital signal represents a binary value, so it can take only one of two allowed levels, while an analogue signal represents a continuous quantity and can take any value in a range. In a CD player the music is stored on the disc as a digital pattern of 1s and 0s, and the digital-to-analogue converter turns that pattern into a continuously varying analogue voltage which drives the loudspeaker.

The essential difference is the number of values the signal can take. A digital signal is a sequence of discrete allowed levels - here binary 0 and 1 - so it can be stored, copied and regenerated without loss and can be processed by digital circuits. An analogue signal varies continuously, taking any value in a range, so it represents a physical quantity directly but cannot be stored or processed without conversion.

In a CD player both kinds of signal appear. The recording on the disc is digital: the sound has been sampled at regular intervals and each sample converted to a binary number, so the disc carries a pattern of pits and lands representing 1s and 0s. The pickups read that pattern, and after digital processing the digital-to-analogue converter converts the binary samples into a continuously varying analogue voltage. That analogue voltage drives the loudspeaker, whose cone must move by a continuously varying amount to reproduce the sound wave. The microphone used to make the recording is the reverse case, converting an analogue signal into a digital one.

items: 2 marks: correctly differentiates between analogue and digital signals and correctly identifies the use of analogue and digital signals in a CD player.
1 mark: makes a correct statement about the characteristics of analogue or digital signals, or about analogue or digital signals in a CD player.

content.text: Analyse how the development of the integrated circuit has affected energy consumption.
Separate the two effects: what happened to the energy used by an individual device, and what happened to the number of devices in the world.
An analysis needs an implication drawn out at the end, not just the two trends stated.

Developing the integrated circuit replaced large circuit boards full of separate components with one small device, so an individual circuit became far smaller, faster and more power-efficient and needed much less energy to manufacture. But the same technology made electronics far cheaper, so vastly more circuits were produced and put into service, and their combined energy consumption rose. Total energy use therefore increased even though each device improved, and it will keep rising as the number of connected devices grows.

Two trends have to be separated. Per device, energy consumption fell sharply. Miniaturisation replaced boards of separate transistors and other components with a single integrated circuit; the fall in the energy needed to switch each transistor as its size shrank, together with the much smaller amount of material and energy needed to fabricate a chip instead of soldering a board, means each circuit now uses far less power and takes far less energy to make than the equivalent circuit of a few decades earlier.

In total, however, energy consumption rose. The same development made electronics dramatically cheaper, so the number of circuits manufactured, and the number in service, increased by orders of magnitude; and because each new device tends to add to the existing ones rather than simply replacing them, the total power demand of households, data centres and industry grew. The fall in energy per function has been outpaced by the growth in the number of functions performed.

The analysis follows from this. A society that judges efficiency only per device will conclude that electronics is becoming steadily more efficient, whereas the total energy drawn by the electronic devices actually in use has grown and will continue to grow as penetration increases. That is the implication the question is looking for, and it is why data-centre energy consumption and the standby power of household electronics have become matters of public policy rather than only of engineering.

items: 3–4 marks: identifies features of the integrated circuit relevant to energy consumption, relates the integrated circuit to energy consumption, and draws out implications.
1–2 marks: identifies features of the integrated circuit relevant to energy consumption, or identifies implications.

content.text: The advancement of silicon-based integrated circuit technology has resulted in progressive miniaturisation and a doubling of circuit performance roughly every 18 months. It is expected that physics limitations will soon halt this progress, requiring a reconceptualisation of the way integrated circuits are constructed.
If this reconceptualisation cannot be realised, what would be the likely impact on society?
First state the physical reason progress must stop - it is the size of atoms and quantum effects, not economics or a lack of demand.
Then trace what society has come to expect from that progress, and what would be lost if the rate of improvement froze while the number of devices kept growing.
Remember to say what would NOT change as well: analogue electronics does not depend on feature size in the same way, so it is not affected to the same degree.

Progress depends on continuing to shrink circuit features, and shrinking is limited by the size of atoms and by quantum effects, so a reconceptualisation of how integrated circuits are built is required. If it cannot be realised, society's expectation of a doubling of performance roughly every 18 months would be unmet: computing and communications performance would freeze, new applications would no longer appear at the present rate, and the economic and social changes driven by them would stall, while the pressure to add more devices continued. Analogue electronics would be much less affected, since its performance is set by discrete components and power-switching requirements rather than by feature size, so it would continue to improve.

The advancement of silicon-based integrated circuit technology rests on the progressive miniaturisation of circuit features: more circuits can be packed into a given area of silicon as the features shrink, and smaller features switch faster and use less power, so processing power, memory capacity and speed all rise together. This has delivered roughly a doubling of performance every 18 months since the late 1960s.

The limit is physical. A feature cannot be made smaller than an atom, and once features approach a few nanometres the electrons in the device are confined on the scale of their own wavelength; quantum tunnelling and quantised energy levels then prevent the reliable switching behaviour on which every logic circuit depends. Physics, not economics or demand, will therefore force a reconceptualisation of how circuits are constructed.

Society is now thoroughly conditioned by this rate. Personal computers, mobile phones, the internet, digital media, satellite navigation and modern medical monitoring all assume steady gains in speed and capacity, and industries have reorganised around that assumption. If the reconceptualisation cannot be realised, performance would stop improving rather than merely improve more slowly: the curve would flatten, new applications would appear far less often, and the further social and economic changes now driven by computing and communications would slow or stop.

Two qualifications matter for a full answer. First, the pressure to add more devices does not disappear, so the number of circuits in use would keep growing while none of them improved further; energy consumption and electronic waste would therefore continue to rise with none of the compensating efficiency gains. Second, analogue electronics would be largely unaffected, because the performance of an analogue circuit is set by the accuracy of its components and by power-switching requirements rather than by lithographic feature size, so it would continue to improve on its own slower trajectory.

items: 5–6 marks: demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding of integrated circuits, provides a detailed description of advancements in silicon-based integrated circuits, relates these to miniaturisation, relates both to physics limitations, discusses current society and what will and will not change if reconceptualisation is not realised, and demonstrates coherence and logical progression.

3–4 marks: demonstrates sound knowledge of integrated circuits, provides a description of advancements and relates to miniaturisation and physics limitations, discusses this with some reference to current society, and communicates scientific ideas clearly.
1–2 marks: demonstrates a basic knowledge of integrated circuits, communicates simple ideas, and provides an outline of advances or attempts to relate reconceptualisation to current society.
